summary.text: Catalysis is the increase in the rate of a chemical reaction caused by an added substance called a catalyst.
A catalyst is not consumed by the reaction: it forms intermediates with reactants and is regenerated, so it remains unchanged afterwards.
It works by giving the reaction an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so more molecular collisions have the energy to reach the transition state.

facts.label: Industry use
facts.value: An estimated 90% of commercial chemical products involve catalysts

facts.label: Word origin
facts.value: Greek kataluein, meaning loosen or untie

facts.label: SI unit of activity
facts.value: The katal, in moles per second

facts.label: Main types
facts.value: Homogeneous and heterogeneous, with enzymes a third category

items.prompt: Hydrogen peroxide solution sits on a shelf. A chemist sprinkles in manganese dioxide and it fizzes with oxygen. What can be done with the powder afterwards?

options.label: It can be recovered unchanged and reused
It is used up, so it must be replaced for each batch
It turns into oxygen along with the rest
It ends up as a new compound that must be thrown away

items.explain: The catalyst is not consumed in the reaction and may be recovered unchanged and re-used indefinitely.

items.prompt: A catalyst is added to a reaction heading for equilibrium. What does it do to the final balance between reactants and products?

options.label: It shifts the balance towards the products
It shifts the balance towards the reactants
Nothing, because it has no effect on the chemical equilibrium
It changes the balance depending on how much catalyst is added

items.explain: Catalysts do not change the extent of a reaction; the ratio of the forward and reverse reaction rates is unaffected.

items.prompt: Could adding a catalyst ever lower the total rate of a reaction?

options.label: Yes, because the catalyst can block the uncatalyzed route entirely
No, because the uncatalyzed route stays possible, the total can only go up
Yes, if too much catalyst is added to the mixture
No, because catalysts speed up only the uncatalyzed route

items.explain: The noncatalyzed mechanism remains possible, so the total rate can only increase in the presence of the catalyst and never decrease.

items.prompt: Hydrogen and oxygen gas react to make water on the surface of titanium dioxide, which acts as the catalyst. What kind of catalysis is this?

options.label: Homogeneous catalysis
Biocatalysis
Nanocatalysis
Heterogeneous catalysis

items.explain: The reaction of oxygen and hydrogen on the surface of titanium dioxide is given as an example of heterogeneous catalysis.

items.prompt: A catalyst makes a reaction faster without being used up. What is the main way it does this?

options.label: It gives a pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions have enough energy
It adds heat to the reaction, so every collision has more energy
It reacts with all the product, so the reaction runs backwards
It makes the reactant particles collide in far greater numbers

items.explain: Catalysts enable pathways with lower activation energy, so more molecular collisions have the energy needed to reach the transition state.

items.prompt: Catalysts are used to tackle air pollution from a poisonous gas. What do they do to that gas?

options.label: They store it so it can be released later
They make it more toxic but easier to see
They help remove it and turn it into useful materials
They only slow its release, without changing it

items.explain: Using catalysts for the hydrogenation of carbon monoxide helps remove this toxic gas and produce useful materials.
